title: Jeremiah 31:15–22
context: The LORD voices a lament heard in Ramah: Rachel, the mother of Joseph and Benjamin and so the ancestress of Ephraim, Manasseh, and Benjamin, weeps for her children and refuses comfort because they are no more (31:15). Ramah lay north of Jerusalem in Benjamin; Jeremiah 40:1 places captives there, and Rachel’s burial is linked in Genesis 35:19 and 1 Samuel 10:2 with places whose exact identification is debated, so the reason for the setting is best held loosely. Matthew 2:17–18 cites this verse at Herod’s killing of the children of Bethlehem; the site’s notes on Matthew 2 treat that use, and the wider consolation of this chapter stands behind it. The LORD answers Rachel: refrain from weeping, for her children will come again from the land of the enemy, and there is hope for her latter end (31:16–17). In 31:18–20 the LORD has heard Ephraim confessing, “Turn me, and I will be turned,” and repenting, and the LORD responds that Ephraim is his dear son and that his heart yearns for him. The prayer to be turned is natural ground for the two traditions to describe grace and repentance differently; the site’s discussions at Deuteronomy 10:16 and Judges 10:16 cover the question and are not restated here. In 31:21–22 the LORD calls the virgin of Israel to set up road signs and return, and announces a new thing: “a woman will encompass a man.” That phrase is notoriously obscure. Readers have suggested a reversal of roles in which the once-faithless woman, Israel, now clings to or seeks the LORD; a picture of security so complete that a woman protects a man; a proverb whose sense is now lost; and, in some older Christian readings, a reference to the virgin conception of Christ. None of these is required by the text, and the notes present them without choosing.

verses.text: The LORD says: “A voice is heard in Ramah, lamentation and bitter weeping, Rachel weeping for her children. She refuses to be comforted for her children, because they are no more.”
verses.arminianNotes: “A voice is heard in Ramah … Rachel weeping for her children. She refuses to be comforted.” Arminian readers hear grief honored, not hurried: the mother of Israel’s tribes mourns the exiled and the dead, and God gives words for real loss. Matthew 2:17–18 cites this lament for the children of Bethlehem, holding grief honestly before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same lament within God’s purposes, and they note that Matthew 2:17–18 sees Israel’s sorrow echoed at the infancy of the Messiah, while the chapter’s consolation stands behind it. Shared ground: both traditions read Rachel as a figure for the mothers of Israel, both hold the setting at Ramah loosely, and both let lament stand before comfort.

verses.text: The LORD says: “Refrain your voice from weeping, and your eyes from tears, for your work will be rewarded,” says the LORD. “They will come again from the land of the enemy.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD answers, “Refrain your voice from weeping … for your work will be rewarded … They will come again from the land of the enemy.” Arminian readers see God tenderly addressing the grieving and promising return, and they read “your work will be rewarded” as assurance that her labor and tears are not wasted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God answering lament with his own promise, so the comfort Rachel refused from others comes from the LORD himself. Shared ground: both traditions read the command to refrain from weeping as comfort grounded in a promise, not a rebuke of grief, and both see the return of the children as the answer to 31:15.

verses.text: There is hope for your latter end,” says the LORD. “Your children will come again to their own territory.
verses.arminianNotes: “There is hope for your latter end … Your children will come again to their own territory.” Arminian readers hear hope offered to a people who had seemed to have no future, an invitation to trust the LORD’s promise and look beyond present loss to restoration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same hope as resting on God’s word rather than on visible signs, a promise he will surely keep for his people. Shared ground: both traditions read “hope for your latter end” as genuine future for the exiles, and both hear in the verse a comfort many Christians also apply to grief more broadly (compare 29:11).

verses.text: “I have surely heard Ephraim grieving thus, ‘You have chastised me, and I was chastised, as an untrained calf. Turn me, and I will be turned, for you are the LORD my God.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD has heard Ephraim say, “You have chastised me … Turn me, and I will be turned, for you are the LORD my God.” Arminian readers see a sincere prayer for God’s enabling grace, which makes repentance possible and to which Ephraim responds, so that turning is both grace-given and genuinely Ephraim’s own.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in “Turn me, and I will be turned” a confession that repentance depends on God’s effectual work, which then truly results in turning (compare Lamentations 5:21). Shared ground: both traditions affirm that grace precedes and enables repentance and that the repentance is real; the deeper question is treated at Deuteronomy 10:16 and Judges 10:16.

verses.text: Surely after that I was turned. I repented. After that I was instructed. I struck my thigh. I was ashamed, yes, even confounded, because I bore the reproach of my youth.’
verses.arminianNotes: Ephraim continues, “Surely after that I was turned. I repented … I struck my thigh. I was ashamed … because I bore the reproach of my youth.” Arminian readers see genuine repentance with grief, instruction, and shame, the response of one who has accepted correction and owns his past sins.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sequence “turned … repented … instructed” as the fruit of God’s turning work in 31:18, with real sorrow and real shame. Shared ground: both traditions read striking the thigh as a gesture of grief or remorse (compare Ezekiel 21:12), and both hold that true repentance includes honest acknowledgment of sin.

verses.text: Is Ephraim my dear son? Is he a darling child? For as often as I speak against him, I still earnestly remember him. Therefore my heart yearns for him. I will surely have mercy on him,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “Is Ephraim my dear son? … as often as I speak against him, I still earnestly remember him. Therefore my heart yearns for him. I will surely have mercy on him.” Arminian readers hear the LORD’s deep and moving love, a yearning that responds to Ephraim’s repentance and shows that God’s mercy is warm and personal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same yearning love, which persisted even while the LORD spoke against Ephraim, and they see mercy rooted in God’s heart rather than in Ephraim’s merit. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as one of Scripture’s tenderest pictures of divine compassion (compare Hosea 11:8), and the site treats God’s emotions at Judges 10:16.

verses.text: “Set up road signs. Make guideposts. Set your heart toward the highway, even the way by which you went. Turn again, virgin of Israel. Turn again to these your cities.
verses.arminianNotes: “Set up road signs. Make guideposts. Set your heart toward the highway … Turn again, virgin of Israel.” Arminian readers hear a real call to action: the exiles must mark the way and set their hearts on returning, responding to God’s promise with resolve and movement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same command as the means by which God brings his people home, with the call to set the heart showing that return is inward as well as outward. Shared ground: both traditions read the road signs as preparation for the journey home along the way they once went into exile, and both hear “Turn again” as repentance and return together.

verses.text: How long will you go here and there, you backsliding daughter? For the LORD has created a new thing on the earth: a woman will encompass a man.”
verses.arminianNotes: “How long will you go here and there, you backsliding daughter? For the LORD has created a new thing … a woman will encompass a man.” Arminian readers hear a rebuke of wavering and a summons to decide. The final phrase is obscure, and readers in this tradition propose several senses without consensus, including Israel now clinging to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the word “created,” marking a new act of God. Proposed readings of “a woman will encompass a man” include a reversal in which faithless Israel seeks the LORD, a picture of complete security, a lost proverb, and, among some older Christian readers, the virgin conception. Shared ground: both traditions hold these readings tentatively, and neither builds doctrine on the phrase.
